passage: 'there is a pronounced increase in spurious correlation between variables when ratios are compounded and the magnitude of this spurious correlation is a function of the size of the denominator coefficient of variation'; the cases include Y = X1/X2 against Z = X3/X2 (abstract, via OpenAlex).
faulty: Pearson correlation of the two ratios Y = head_width/body_length and Z = wing_length/body_length over the 2000 specimens; criterion r >= 0.30. Source parameters: X1, X2, X3 continuous; the correlation between the ratios grows with the coefficient of variation of the denominator X2 (from r = 0.0 between raw variables up to r = 0.99 between ratios).
fixed: Partial correlation of head_width and wing_length given body_length (correlate the residuals of each on body_length, with intercept); criterion >= 0.30.
estimand: Faulty: correlation between two size-standardised ratios, which contains the variation of the common denominator. Fixed: correlation between head width and wing length after the linear effect of body length is removed from both.
model_family: Source's simulation family: independent continuous variables X1, X2, X3 (normal for the numerators, positive-skew e.g. lognormal for the denominator X2) with the denominator coefficient of variation as the controlled parameter. Claim-true world adds a latent factor shared by X1 and X3 net of X2. Chosen because the source names only continuous variables with a varied denominator CV; fixed for both twins.
sizes_note: Source: minimum simulation sample size 25,000, which exceeds the 2000 cap; 2000 (the cap) is used and the check of the fixed analysis (two regressions on 2000 values) takes seconds. Source on size dependence: the spurious correlation is 'a function of the size of the denominator coefficient of variation'; dependence on sample size not stated.
exploited_structure: A denominator that varies across specimens (large coefficient of variation) is divided into both numerators, so the two ratios move together whatever the numerators do.

structure_statistic.note_value_source: source states none: the abstract says the effect grows with the denominator CV but gives no value; 0.15 is a realistic coefficient of variation of adult body length in a single species, and is enough for the ratio correlation to be large when numerator CVs are about 0.1

notes: Pair case (ATC76 slot 1 of 2 pairs). Statistic family correlation; ATC76 has no earlier combinations. Differs from B3B-02 (slope, per-population structure) and B3B-11 (other, matrix of traits).
